messages.body_plain:
I have a dataset with a fixed number of units observed at repeated points in time.  What is the best way to introduce time-invariant and time-variant graphs?

Let's say we had 100 units observed at 5 points in time.  One could imagine the following formula:

y ~ t + f(idu, model = 'generic1', Cmatrix = TIV),

where y is a time-varying outcome, t represents time (i.e. we assume a linear trend), idu = rep(1:100, 6), and TIV is a 100 x 100 matrix depicting time-invariant adjacencies among each of the 100 units.  When I use real data, this works about as I would expect.

I also tried to estimate the same model using the following specification:

y ~ t + f(idut, model = 'generic1', Cmatrix = TIV.BD <http://TIV.BD>),

where y and t are the same as before, idut = 1:500, and TIV.BD <http://TIV.BD> is a block diagonal matrix with TIV repeated 5 times along the diagonal.  This is a pretty straightforward way of setting a time-space model using a time-invariant graph.  When I specify the model this way, I get vary different estimates for the beta parameter.

My goal is to introduce a time-varying graph.  I had assumed I could do this using the block diagonal strategy, but given the behavior observed in the time-invariant example, I don't feel confident in this approach.

Am I missing something about the graphs are being treated?  Is there a better way to set up this type of model?  The goal is to estimate a single spatial effect while allowing adjacencies to change over time.

Any help would be much appreciated.

Working example below using the Georgia data.  The models aren't perfect, but the basic concept should be clear:

#libraries
library(maptools)
library(sp)
library(spdep)
library(INLA)
library(Matrix)

#load spatial data
georgia <- readShapePoly("co13_d00.shp")
ga.dslv <- unionSpatialPolygons(georgia, georgia@data$NAME)

#load tabular data
d <- read.csv('data.final.csv')
d <- d[match(names(ga.dslv), d$X),]
dg.rs <- reshape(d, idvar = 'X', varying = 2:NCOL(d),
                 v.names = c('obs', 'Exp'), times = 2000:2010,
                 direction = 'long')

#dimensions
NT <- NROW(dg.rs)
N <- NROW(ga.dslv)

#generate id
dg.rs$idu <- rep(1:N, NT / N)
dg.rs$idut <- dg.rs$idut2 <- 1:NT

#generate matrices
B <- nb2mat(poly2nb(ga.dslv), style = 'B')
I <- diag(NROW(B))
R <- -B
diag(R) <- rowSums(B)
C <- I - R
dimnames(C) <- list(1:NROW(B), 1:NROW(B))
C.BD <http://C.BD> <- kronecker(diag(NT / N), C)

#define drop function
tiedrop <- function(B) {
  mat <- B
  ndrop <- (sum(B) / 2) * .15
  tie.loc <- which(B == 1, arr.ind = TRUE)
  tie.drop <- tie.loc[sample(tie.loc, trunc(ndrop)), ]
  B[tie.drop[, 1], tie.drop[, 2]] <- 0
  B[tie.drop[, 2], tie.drop[, 1]] <- 0
  B
}

#generate time-varying matrices by randomly dropping 15 percent of ties
B.DYN <- bdiag(lapply(1:(NT / N), function(x) tiedrop(B)))
I.DYN <- diag(NROW(B.DYN))
R.DYN <- -B.DYN
diag(R.DYN) <- rowSums(B.DYN)
C.DYN <- I.DYN - R.DYN

#model
mf.c <- obs ~ time + f(idu, model = 'generic1', Cmatrix = C)
mf.c.bd <http://mf.c.bd> <- obs ~ time + f(idut, model = 'generic1', Cmatrix = C.BD <http://C.BD>)
mf.c.dyn <- obs ~ time + f(idut, model = 'generic1', Cmatrix = C.DYN)
mf.comb <- obs ~ time +
  f(idut, model = 'generic1', Cmatrix = C.BD <http://C.BD>) +
  f(idut2, model = 'generic1', Cmatrix = C.DYN)

mod.c <- inla(mf.c, E = Exp, data = dg.rs, family = "poisson")
mod.c.bd <http://mod.c.bd> <- inla(mf.c.bd <http://mf.c.bd>, E = Exp, data = dg.rs, family = "poisson")
mod.c.dyn <- inla(mf.c.dyn, E = Exp, data = dg.rs, family = "poisson")
mod.c.comb <- inla(mf.comb, E = Exp, data = dg.rs, family = "poisson")

Dear Help,

 I am using INLA to fit a model of the negative binomial family with log-link to some time series. My goal is to obtain a quantile of the predictive posterior distribution of the response variable y_t.

My current code works but I wonder if I could make it faster.

Right now, after I have fit the model using INLA, I compute the quantile through Monte Carlo sampling. I draw random samples (inla.rmarginal) from the marginal for the mean of the negative binomial distribution (marginals.fitted.values) and for the overdispersion parameter theta (internal.marginals.hyperpar[[1]]). I draw mc.mutheta values of the mean and of the parameter theta. This gives me mc.mutheta (mean,theta)_j. For each of them I draw mc.y values from the negative binomial distribution parameterized by (mean,theta)_j. Thus I get a vector of mc.mutheta*mc.y values for the response, upon which I apply the quantile() function to get the quantile of the posterior predictive distribution I want. This is quite compute-intensive.

Therefore my question use: is there a faster way in INLA to get the quantile of the predictive posterior distribution of the response variable or to sample from this distribution?

Thanks a lot in advance!

Best wishes

Maëlle.

sorry for late response.

This model says that the 'idu' effect is constant over time, and the
time effect is linear in the mean.

> I also tried to estimate the same model using the following

This is the same as the 'replicate' feature, meaning that the 'idu'
effect is (conditional) independent in time, and you have one
realisation for each time point.

This kind of extention is already there, like

y ~ t + f(idu, model = 'generic1', Cmatrix = TIV, replicate = tim)

where tim is assumed to be 1 for year 1, 2 for year 2 and so on. See

http://www.r-inla.org/models/tools#TOC-Replicate-a-model

for details.

>   This is a pretty straightforward way of setting a time-space model
> using a time-invariant graph.  When I specify the model this way, I
> get vary different estimates for the beta parameter.

yes, this is a very different model.

> My goal is to introduce a time-varying graph.  I had assumed I could
> do this using the block diagonal strategy, but given the behavior
> observed in the time-invariant example, I don't feel confident in this
> approach.

time-varying 'graphs' is not something that is supported, nor is easy to
do (unless you can do it with the generic model, but this is veryyy
restrictive and not what you want i guess)

> Am I missing something about the graphs are being treated?  Is there a
> better way to set up this type of model?  The goal is to estimate a
> single spatial effect while allowing adjacencies to change over time.

You have not missed the point. Estimating the graph itself and how it
changes is difficult in the sense that there is little information in
the data about this, hence it boils down to prior modeling. Also, we do
not support these models as they are outside our latent-gaussian-model
class (or the practical subset of these), hence you are on your own.
you may have to impose strong sparsity to get something 'sensible' out I
presume, but this will also depend on the type of data you have and
other model considerations.

On 12/08/14 04:39, Mike Gahan wrote:
> Would it be overly ambitious to attempt to create this raster surface with all 1 million observations?

The raster resolution is not related to the dimension of your data. You can estimate such surface in high or small resolution with few or larger number of observations. The main limitation is the number of basis functions, related to number of mesh triangles.

> The process to create the mesh is taking quite a while (I admit that I do not understand the best
> way to create this mesh).  Does anyone have suggestions on the best way to go about creating the mesh
> object?  I have been making my way through the spde tutorial and I am a bit confused on the parameters
> to this function.

The main argument is max.edge=c(a,b), where
  a = maximum length of the inner edges
  b = maximum length of the outer edges
So, you can have a mesh with few triangles when you set 'a' and 'b' bigger and you can have a mesh with more triangles setting they smaller values. An important argument is the 'cuttof', used to avoid small triangles.

For non-convex shaped domains, it is good to consider using the inla.nonconvex.hull() function before creating the mesh. Please consider the following examples:

require(maps)
us <- map("usa", fill=TRUE, col="transparent", plot=FALSE)
IDs <- sapply(strsplit(us$names, ":"), function(x) x[1])

require(sp)
prj <- CRS("+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84")

require(maptools)
sp <- map2SpatialPolygons(us, IDs=IDs, proj4string=prj)

### first way: using the polygon
require(INLA)
pl.bound <- inla.sp2segment(sp)

mesh0 <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=pl.bound, max.edge=c(3,7), cutoff=1)

### second way: using the location points
## suppose you have these points:
require(splancs)
pts <- csr(sp@polygons[[3]]@Polygons[[1]]@coords, 1e5)

require(INLA)
pt.bond <- inla.nonconvex.hull(pts, 2, 2)
pt.bond2 <- inla.nonconvex.hull(pts, 1, 1, 100)

mesh1 <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=pt.bond, max.edge=c(5,10), cut=1)
mesh2 <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=pt.bond, max.edge=c(3,7), cut=1)
mesh3 <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=pt.bond2, max.edge=c(2,4), cut=1, off=c(1e-5,4))

c(mesh0$n, mesh1$n, mesh2$n, mesh3$n)

par(mfrow=c(2,2), mar=c(0,0,1,0))
plot(mesh0, asp=1)
plot(mesh1, asp=1)
plot(mesh2, asp=1)
plot(mesh3, asp=1)

best,
Elias.

I'm new to INLA so I was hoping I could post a follow up to better understand inla.posterior.sample. I have a model with fixed effects, temporal autocorrelation (AR1 model), and spatial autocorrelation (Besag model). I have 2900 "observations" in my data (some are NAs for predictive purposes). The latent posterior samples for my model have 2900 "Predictor.xxxx" samples, 2900 "ID.xxxx" samples, and 2900 "year.xxxx" samples, where ID and year are the replicates for the AR1 and Besag models, respectively, plus the coefficients for the intercept and covariate for the fixed effects.

Are the "Predictor.xxxx" samples the "fitted values" from the joint posterior and the "ID.xxxx" and "year.xxxx" the estimated error for their respective models?

Adam

messages.subject: Lognormal prior for fixed effect parameter
messages.subject_clean: Lognormal prior for fixed effect parameter
messages.body_plain:
I need to restrict the values of a fixed effect parameter to only negative values.  The parameter is the regression coefficient for the quadratic effect of one of the explanatory variables in a random slope Poisson regression with an ar1 model for the random effects.  Without such a restrictions the posterior distributions for other quantities of interest (which involve this parameter in the denominator) would basically not make much sense.  So the idea would be to build this restriction into the prior (perhaps after first checking if a negative quadratic effect is supported by the data).

I'm aware of the control.fixed argument which could be used to specify normal priors on the fixed effects but we think it would make more sense (within the biological context) to think about this parameter as a form of scale parameter which would suggest that a vague lognormal prior (for the negative value) may be more sensible.

To implement this, we are currently sampling from the joint posterior using inla.posterior.sample() and then using rejecting sampling such that the resulting distribution corresponds to our desired choice of prior.  This is obviously somewhat inefficient however if using a large variance for the lognormal making the rejection probability very high.

So I'm wondering if there is any other way getting around this problem?

Jarle Tufto

The current version of this function (from the July 4 inla version) seems to have some strange behaviour.  Here is a fairly minimal example plotting samples from the joint marginal of the hyperparameters of the ar1 part of a model:

n = 1000
rho = 0.8

y=rpois(n,10*exp(eta))
data = list(y=y,z=1:n)
formula = y~f(z,model="ar1")
result = inla(formula,family="poisson", data = data, control.compute=list(config=TRUE))
nsim <- 1000
sample <- inla.posterior.sample(nsim,result)
x <- matrix(NA,nsim,2)
for (i in 1:nsim) x[i,] <- sample[[i]]$hyperpar
plot(x)

 <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-oCePIAlk7as/U_SMPjFTkzI/AAAAAAAAAYs/EjsOMFsqMOc/s1600/Rplot.png>
So, the sample just contain 9 unique values for the hyperparameters.  I suppose this is not intended behaviour?

Best regards,
Jarle

Jarle

Hi,

In the full Bayesian analysis, the marginal posterior distribution at a location isn't actually Gaussian, and inla instead computes it as a mixture of Gaussians.  Sampling from the posterior can then be used for full posterior predictions.

If you instead do an "empirical Bayes" analysis (strategy="eb"), _then_ the posterior distributions are Gaussian, like you discuss.  In this case, adding the squared prediction sd and the estimated observation variance will give the data prediction variance.

Finn L

Dear INLA forum,

We would like to implement a model such as

y = M %*% beta + G %*% b

where M and G are matrices, beta fixed regression coefficients and b individuals effects which are random.

The problem is that beta is a vector of fixed effects and b has to be a vector which includes random effects. We have written the following code but in this we would be introducing all the effects as if they were random. How can we fix it?

M <- cbind(X,G%*%Z)
y = M %*% beta + G %*% b
weight.beta <- c(1,25)
Qz <- diag(1,dim(G)[2])
nb <- dim(M)[2]
nz <- dim(G)[2]

idx.beta = c(1:nb, rep(NA, nz))
idx.b = c(rep(NA, nb), 1:nz)
hyper.fixed = list(prec = list(initial = log(0.001), fixed=TRUE))
formula = Y ~ -1 + f(idx.beta,  model="iid", hyper = hyper.fixed, constr = FALSE)+ f(idx.b, model="generic", Cmatrix=Qz)
result = inla(formula, family = "binomial", data = list(y=Y, idx.beta=idx.beta, idx.b=idx.b), control.predictor = list(A=cBind(M, G)))

Thank you very much,

Laura
